title: The comb
hookLine: Buson: a piercing chill, stepping on my dead wife's comb in the bedroom
tomorrow: a flower takes the well bucket. what does the poet do for water?

lines: THE RECEIPT IN THE COAT POCKET.
A COLD THAT GOES RIGHT THROUGH.
cards: Clearing out after someone dies, the big furniture is rarely the hard part. It's the receipt in a coat pocket, the voicemail nobody can delete.
The painter and poet Buson put it in one breath: mi ni shimu ya, naki tsuma no kushi wo, neya ni fumu. A cold that goes right through me: in our bedroom, I step on my dead wife's comb.

teach.b: So what do you do with the comb? Buddhism gives two honest answers, and they pull in different directions. View one comes from an old story.
A young mother, Kisa Gotami, carries her dead child from house to house, begging for medicine. The Buddha tells her to bring a mustard seed from a home where no one has ever died.
She knocks on door after door and finds none. Then she sets the child down and understands: loss is in every house. Clinging, the Buddha taught, is what turns loss into suffering.
The best case for this view: the comb is not his wife, and gripping it can keep the wound open. View two lives in Buddhist homes in Japan.
A family may keep a butsudan, a household altar, with the names of their dead on memorial tablets. They offer incense and rice, and tell the dead about the day.
At Obon, the summer festival, they light lanterns to welcome the dead home. The best case for this view: the bond doesn't end at death, and tending it is a practice of gratitude.
One view says loosen the grip.
The other says keep a place set.
It only shows how far a small comb can reach.

how: In Japan, Buddhist families may keep a butsudan with memorial tablets, offering incense and food, and welcome the dead home at Obon. Buddhist teaching also tells the story of Kisa Gotami to show that loss comes to every house.

o: a wedding gift that a groom gives his bride in Japan
a small keepsake of the dead, stepped on in Buson's poem
a monk's rake for combing sand in a temple garden

games.q: two answers to the comb: tap the pairs.
p: sought a seed from a house with no death
household altar with the names of the dead
summer festival welcoming the dead home

s: Buddhism teaches you to get rid of a loved one's belongings
Kisa Gotami's story teaches loosening the grip; the butsudan keeps the names of the dead at home. both are Buddhist.
at Obon, families in Japan light lanterns to welcome the dead home
the summer festival of the dead.
Buson's poem tells you what to do with grief
it shows the cold of one small comb and leaves the choice to you.

games.q: your friend keeps her late dad's coat on the hook and won't move it. you lean toward 'let go.' what's the strongest case for her side?
o: keeping a place for the dead is Buddhist too: the butsudan tends the bond.
she just isn't ready yet, and she'll let go later.
the coat holds his spirit, so moving it would hurt him.
games.why: the best case for keeping isn't 'not ready yet': Buddhist homes in Japan tend their dead at the butsudan as a practice of its own.

practice: If you have something small that belonged to someone you've lost, or someone far away, hold it or picture it. Look at it first as an object: its color, its weight, the wear on it.
Then let it be what it is to you, and set it down gently when the quiet ends.

wordCard.voice: The comb: a small thing underfoot in Buson's poem, and the old question of what we keep.
